summary:
Same-sex conduct has been criminalised in Gambia since historic-era rule, retained from the 1933 Criminal Code implemented in 1934 as carnal knowledge against the order of nature. Section 158 previously punished homosexual acts by up to 14 years imprisonment for men and women, after the Criminal Code (Amendment) Act 2005 extended gross indecency to women. The Criminal Code (Amendment) Act signed in October 2014 created aggravated homosexuality carrying mandatory life imprisonment for serial offenders, for gay or lesbian people living with HIV, for acts with persons under 18, with disabled or drugged persons, or where the accused was a parent, guardian or authority figure. That life clause was removed by the Criminal Code adopted in March 2025, which instead imposes a five-year minimum sentence for unnatural offences defined in statute as any homosexual act with no stated maximum, and three years for gross indecency.

Gender expression is separately restricted. Since 2013 section 167 of the Criminal Code forbids men to dress as women, punishable by up to five years imprisonment or a fine of 50,000 Gambian dalasi. Gambia makes no provision for official change of gender and citizens cannot change legal gender. No law or regulation protects residents against discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity.

Same-sex couples have no legal recognition in Gambia. LGBTQ people are prohibited from adopting children.

Enforcement under the current framework is active. The Barrow government has not typically enforced the provisions and promised not to prosecute same-sex couples for consensual sexual acts, while stating there are no plans for liberalisation. The United States Department of State reported arrests and societal discrimination in 2020 and no prosecutions but continued stigma and police harassment in 2021. On 5 March 2026 the Brusubi Magistrates Court sentenced Muhammad Jawo and Muhammad Krubally each to five years imprisonment for violation of section 147(1) for indecent conduct between men in an unfinished building.

Foreign visitors have been directly targeted under these laws. On 15 May 2008 President Yahya Jammeh gave homosexuals 24 hours to leave the country and ordered the Inspector General of Police and the director of the Gambia Immigration Department to conduct mass patrols, warning that any hotel, lodge or motel lodging such persons would be closed. He also vowed to cut off the head of any homosexual and threatened dismissal of gay soldiers. In June 2008 two Spanish men in their 50s alleged to be gay were arrested and detained at Kotu police station after taxi drivers reported them, and were released after intervention by the Spanish government. On 23 December 2008 Frank Boers, a 79-year-old Dutch national, was arrested at Banjul International Airport when officials found pornography including nude photos of himself and Gambian men in his possession, and was convicted of indecency and fined 100,000 dalasis in lieu of a two-year sentence.

Gender non-conformity has been policed. Human Rights Watch reports regular organised actions by law enforcement against persons suspected of gender non-conformity. On 10 April 2012 police arrested 18 men at a bar in the Tourism Development Area, 16 Senegalese, one Gambian and one Nigerian, for indecent practice after testifying the men were wearing women's clothes, carrying handbags and walking like ladies. A court remanded the men and the prosecutor dropped all charges on 1 August 2012. In November 2014 state forces launched an investigation under the aggravated law producing at least eight arrests, including at least four adult men, a 17-year-old boy and nine women, with three more men interrogated in December 2014. Detainees were held at the National Intelligence Agency headquarters in Banjul and allegedly tortured and ill-treated to compel confessions. Arrests are believed to have been common during the Jammeh presidency, though data is lacking.

Societal risk remains severe. A 2021 to 2023 survey found 93 percent of Gambians would dislike or strongly dislike having a homosexual neighbour. The media promotes misinformation and harmful stereotypes toward LGBTQ people. There are no LGBTQ organizations in the country after 2016 because it is considered too dangerous, which leaves visitors without local support structures. In 2023 there were reports of healthcare workers refusing to honour LGBTQ people's privacy, which negatively impacted HIV care for LGBTQ Gambians. The 2014 life sentence for gay or lesbian people living with HIV created a direct barrier to testing and treatment.
tangentialFactors:
Freedom House rated Gambia Partly Free at 50 of 100 in Freedom in the World 2024. Political freedoms improved under President Adama Barrow after 22 years of rule by President Jammeh, with severe discrimination against LGBT people listed among ongoing concerns. President Barrow has stated that homosexuality is not an issue in Gambia, with officials downplaying any liberalisation.

Documentation of the prior enforcement climate includes the Human Rights Watch report State of Fear of September 2015, which recorded arbitrary arrests, torture and killings under Jammeh, including his anti-gay rhetoric and explicit threats against LGBT people. That climate is distinct from the current Code but evidences the origin of the statutes visitors now face.
localsOnly:
Many LGBTQ Gambians fear arrest or killing and flee to other countries. Religious leaders are widely opposed, with some calling for LGBTQ people to be killed. Safety concerns likely prevent LGBT testimony to the Truth, Reconciliation and Reparations Commission.

Children are raised within strict male and female gender norms, with non-conformity to the expected heterosexual norm treated as deviant and taboo. Reported employment discrimination affects LGBTQ Gambians.

No incidents of conversion therapy or of surgeries on intersex children or non-consenting adults were reported in the sources reviewed.
outOfScopeNotes:
It is unresolved how frequently arrests occurred during the Jammeh presidency beyond the documented cases, as sources state data is lacking. It is not sourced whether entry, visa, airport screening beyond the 2008 case, or access to sex-segregated facilities impose distinct written rules for trans visitors.

It is not sourced what societal tolerance toward transgender people specifically is. Available survey and media findings concern homosexual neighbours and LGBTQ people in general and must not be conflated with transgender-specific attitudes.
